content: Kykeon (from the Greek word κῠκᾰ́ω, meaning to stir or to mix) was an ancient Greek beverage primarily composed of water, barley, and herbs. It held a significant role in the Eleusinian Mysteries, where it was consumed at the climax of the sacred rituals to break a ceremonial fast. Beyond its religious use, kykeon was also a popular drink among Greek peasants. The drink is referenced in Homeric texts. In the Iliad, kykeon is described as a mixture of barley, water, herbs, and ground goat cheese (Book XV, lines 638–641). In the Odyssey, the sorceress Circe enhances the drink by adding honey and infusing it with her magical potion (Book X, line 234). In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, the goddess Demeter rejects red wine but accepts kykeon made from water, barley, and pennyroyal. Kykeon was believed to have digestive properties. In Aristophanes' play Peace (line 712), Hermes recommends it to the protagonist who has overindulged in dried fruits and nuts. However, the drink was often dismissed by the aristocracy as a beverage of the lower classes. Theophrastus, in his work Characters (Chapter IV, lines 2–3), portrays a peasant whose breath, scented with thyme from kykeon, annoys his neighbors at the Ecclesia (the public assembly). In an effort to understand how participants in the Eleusinian Mysteries consistently reported profound, revelatory experiences over a span of two millennia, some researchers have hypothesized that the barley used in the Eleusinian kykeon may have been contaminated with ergot, a parasitic fungus. Ergot contains psychoactive compounds, which could potentially explain the intense spiritual and visionary states described by those who partook in the ceremonies at Eleusis. However, modern attempts to recreate kykeon using ergot have produced inconclusive results. For further exploration of the potential psychoactive properties of kykeon, one may refer to entheogenic theories related to the Eleusinian Mysteries.
